text: You can already compute a complex number's modulus directly from its real and imaginary parts. There's a second way to get the same answer — multiplying a number by its mirror image — and that second route is the exact calculation quantum computing uses to turn amplitudes into probabilities.

The complex conjugate of z equals a plus b i, written z star, flips the sign of the imaginary part only: z star equals a minus b i. Multiply a complex number by its own conjugate and the cross terms cancel exactly, while the i squared term flips sign and becomes positive — the result is a squared plus b squared, a real number with no i left at all, and it's always zero or positive, since it's a sum of two squares.

Take z equals 3 plus 4i again, so z star is 3 minus 4i. Multiplying them out directly gives 9 plus 16, which is 25. Compare that to the modulus route: the modulus of z is 5, so its square is also 25. Both routes give exactly the same number — confirming that the modulus squared always equals the conjugate times the original.

A qubit's amplitude is a complex number, and later in this course you'll learn the Born rule: a measurement probability equals the squared modulus of the amplitude. You now know exactly how that gets computed in practice — multiply the amplitude by its own conjugate, and the result is guaranteed to be real and non-negative, exactly the property a valid probability needs.
Next lesson puts a vector of complex numbers to the use you've been building toward all chapter: describing the actual state of a single qubit.
